utterances.text: Well, there appears, certainly, to be a mismatch between the status of command and who Mr. Mahmuljin is working for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I may, please, General, draw your attention to what is written under "2" in the very same document, where it says: "The use of the unit-enjoined struggle against the Chetniks and the manner of its resubordination to the 3rd Corps Command." Does the word "resubordination" imply that this unit was previously subordinated to 3rd Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The exhibit can please be removed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was an issue, General, and there were questions about disarming the Mujahedin. Two questions: Would it have made sense for Hadzihasanovic to approach the Mujahedin who were operating in his area of responsibility and in conjunction with his forces? Would it have made sense?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have made sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Hadzihasanovic at the time, did he have the military means to disarm the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did have the military means to do it. There were military police and others who could have done it, and it could have been done in a fairly abrupt manner, if necessary. I think he had that authority from Delic, if necessary, to use force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your view and based on what you got to know and what you've seen, did he have the means to do so prior, including prior to the letter from Delic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you were shown quite a number of documents by my learned friends from the Defence. Do these letters change your views, your views you expressed yesterday, in respect to the use of Mujahedin within 3rd Corps and by 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two elements in that: The first is I find it very strange if General Hadzihasanovic wanted to get my agreement and help with the Mujahedin that he did not show me some very, very serious documents and the correspondence he was having. Now, he didn't have to disclose it, but had he disclosed it, it might have made a difference. On the other hand, as I have mentioned before - and I thought we might have discussed it a little bit further this morning - is this question of using the Mujahedin and the way they do their business and deception and the propaganda tool they represent and the combat multiplier of their use on the battlefield. Whether they were there or not I think was a great help to them and a problem because of the international dimension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my very last question, General: Do the documents that were shown to you by the Defence, do they change in any way your yesterday's comments and your yesterday's testimony in respect to the out-of-control excuse used by Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't change my view at all. If it is a priority that they are to be removed, then you should deal with that priority, temporarily change the task, get it sorted, and get back to your main effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Defence exceptionally like to be given leave to ask some more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to be granted exceptional leave to ask a couple of questions with regard to what the general said in the last line, since the general has to a certain extent contradicted what he told me with regard to whether General Hadzihasanovic had the means to take action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead and ask your questions. Further cross-examination by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You said that the first thing you will do if you are to take on someone, if you are to attack someone, is you have to know who that enemy is and what the force and what is the strength and where this enemy is and who the enemy is. Would you agree with me that this is something that any army commander before launching an attack will identify who the enemy is, and that is the first things that identified in any military order in the world? Would that be a fact, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. He may wish to make sure he's got his force protection in place before he does that. That's not a guarantee. If you're trying to say it's important to identify your target, that's absolutely right. But it's clear from the pieces of paper I've seen that there was a recognised problem with the Mujahedin which people knew about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you are responsible for training the complete British Army. Are you telling me that you're going to tell the British Army that it would be okay to launch an attack without knowing who the enemy is?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that if in any written order in the world, that the first thing is situation and then, which includes as the first thing, the enemy and who the enemy is?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be included as the first thing, yes. It's not obligatory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General, you did not know -- you had no information about the Mujahedin, in terms of who they were, what the money was, what the resupply was, how many there was, how many units there was, where they were, who were their chief, what their relationship with the region was, you knew nothing about that. How can you today come in this courtroom and say that General Hadzihasanovic had the power to take on an unknown enemy that you don't even know who this enemy is? Please comment on this question, General.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said on a number of occasions that I'm not sure they existed or were used, but the fact that they were around was a powerful tool to be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying, General, that you take back your comment --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't take back my comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know for a fact that he could take this problem --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying it was part of a very, very good-class deception plan and very useful for them to use it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question put to you, General, was did he have the military means and was it proper for him to take on the Mujahedin? Your answer was yes. I put it to you that you have no information whatsoever that could allow you to make a judgement here in this courtroom today in replacement of what General Hadzihasanovic could do on the place, in the circumstances at the time, according to his evaluation and assessment of the situation. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have shown me papers which implied there was a great problem for the 3rd Corps with the Mujahedin --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have a question, because the two other Judges don't have any questions for you. I have a question, but it is in another area. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has produced an interview that you had for a magazine. In this interview, which I am quoting from by memory, you indicated that in your house you were visited by representatives of the international press - CNN, World News, Sky News, ZDF, and others - and relations with the press according to you were good, they didn't cause any problems, but you made certain observations off the record. When you met the press, did your authorities know about it or was that also off the record in relation to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it's my experience that any comment to the press is not on the record -- sorry, is not off the record. Any comment to press will be used in future by them. I had very little support from the UK at that time, and on my second day in command I discovered 13 television lenses pointing at me and therefore there was high pressure. I made a point of getting to know the press not to get them on my side but to make sure they understood as much of my task and what I was trying to do as they could. I occasionally, perhaps once every fortnight, had a personal brief with them. The day-to-day handling of my press was done by a senior major appointed for that task and trained for it. But just occasionally, it was quite useful for me to have a one-to-one chat with them and I realised that anything I said to them could be published, because that is the nature of press nowadays. So does that make it clear or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know that the 3rd Corps also had a press centre and the number was 410-349? Did you have contacts with press officers of the 3rd Corps precisely to exchange information with them?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- sir, I don't believe we did have direct contact with members of the press corps -- from the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges have no additional questions. Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I note -- and I noticed that the witness was interrupted to conclude his comments on a question which was asked by my learned friends from the Defence, and I refer to page 47, lines 20 to 24. And I think the general, the witness was asked whether Hadzihasanovic had any means to deal with the Mujahedin issue. I would like that the general be given a possibility to finish his comments, but I would certainly leave it to my friends from the Hadzihasanovic Defence to re-ask the question and to allow the general, the witness, to finish his comments, since he didn't have the chance to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To save time, I'm going to put the question to the witness directly. In response to the Prosecution, you said that the 3rd Corps had the means to deal with this situation of the Mujahedin. The Defence put another question to you, and the Chamber didn't consider it necessary for you to reconfirm it. But as this is a crucial issue, I'm asking you once again: Did the 3rd Corps have the means to resolve the problem of the Mujahedin? Specifically, in view of the fact that there was an order that was shown to you which said that if necessary they should be disarmed. So we would like to have your response as a military officer of great experience.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. I believe it is a matter of priorities. If you are fighting on a number of fronts and some major event occurs inside your organisation or inside your territorial area of responsibility that is causing you huge problems, it may well be that you have to say, "Right, I have to pull out the thorn in my side so I can carry out fighting this battle. And I must do it as quickly and as efficiently as possible." And so I believed -- and looking at the 3rd Corps and my knowledge of the 3rd Corps, that they had the means to take this thorn, the Mujahedin, and get rid of them and then carry on fighting the battle. Because later on during that year there is mention made of Mujahedin doing actions and various other things. If they wanted to remove it, it should have been moved up in their priorities and done as quickly as possible. Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for that clarification. The Chamber wishes to thank you for coming to The Hague to testify over a period of two days. We wish you a safe journey home and best wishes in the continuation of your military career. Thank you. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to be kind enough to escort you out of the courtroom. Unless Mr. Withopf has something to add. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Not in respect to the testimony of the witness. The witness can be taken out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor in a moment. But regarding the documents, Mr. Bourgon, have you had time to think them over, think about them? To assist you, we have 24 documents in this binder. Apparently several have already been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to ask for the tendering of the following documents: On the list that we have, the fifth document; that is, the order from the Bosanska Krajina Operational Group dated the 5th of July, 1993. Also, document number 6, that is, the complaint that was recognised by the witness as a complaint that he made to the HVO regarding the incident with the UNHCR truck. Then I go on to number 23; it is an article written by the witness entitled "Operating in Bosnia." Colonel Duncan is the author and it is dated June 1994. Those are the only three documents, Mr. President, that we would wish to be admitted. The others have either already been admitted or we are not asking them to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, regarding the tendering of documents 5, 6, and 23, no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar -- You have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. A detail. Document number 12, I said that it bore the number P158. In fact, it is DH73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Registrar, three numbers for documents 5, 6, and 23.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document "Order from OGBK" gets Exhibit Number DH171. The document "Formal complaint, HVO activities" gets the exhibit number DH172. And the document "Operating --" the newspaper article "Operating in Bosnia" gets the exhibit number DH173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This actually deals with the break. I would respectfully request to have a break of about 45 minutes to rearrange my documents for the document discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume at half past 11.00. Are there any problems regarding the additional time for the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't understand what we intend to do. We have five or ten documents. I have nothing against 45 minutes, but is there something new that I am not aware of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr. Withopf, what was envisaged was for Mr. Bourgon to take the floor to discuss five examples that he has; then Mr. Dixon, who grouped the documents into categories, will take the floor. Of course, the Prosecution will respond. And does that mean that you intend to produce other documents after the Defence? Because -- what is the reason for which you are asking for this additional time? 45 minutes in all. You need three-quarters of an hour to do what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no intention to discuss any further documents as the ones which have been indicated by my learned friends from the Defence. Mr. President, you certainly do understand that I wish to briefly thank the witness who just left the courtroom, and then I have to take care of the documents. I have to bring down -- That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. I see. It is quarter to 11.00. We will resume in exactly three-quarters of an hour, which means at half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to Mr. Bourgon, I shall give the floor once again to the registrar, because apparently there seems to be an error with the numbering of the documents. Mr. Registrar, will you give us the numbers for those three documents once again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. There was a mistake in the transcript of the 11th of May, 2004 on page 7170. The 10 daily reports drafted by the witness Gerritsen and tendered by Ms. Residovic got a wrong number. The right number must be DH171 and not DH170. As a consequence, the document "Order from OGBK" tendered today cannot get Exhibit Number DH171, but must get the next free number, which is DH174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we hear the three new numbers for the documents; the first, the order of the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group; the document of the 31st of May, and the document of 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the "formal complaint HVO" gets the exhibit number DH172; then the newspaper article titled "Operating Bosnia" get it is exhibit number DH173; and the order of OGBK gets the exhibit number DH174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I only have a few documents on which I should like to make a few observations for the Chamber this morning. I shall begin with document 157 - that was according to the latest numbering used by the Prosecution. It is a document dated the 15th of April, whereas on the list we are told that the date of the document is the 25th of April. Perhaps it would be a good idea, Mr. President, if my learned friend from the Prosecution has the original, because I have a few observations to make regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, do you have the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have the original, and it can be handed over to my learned friend from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I now have the original in my hands - which is a photocopy, actually. In the archives they had a photocopy - and this document bears a stamp coming from the Zagreb archives. In this particular case, I should like to show this document to the Chamber to be able to make a few observations about it. Briefly, the remarks of the Defence are similar to those already made with respect to the use by the Chamber of this document without the assistance of a witness. This is a document coming from the Croatian Defence Council, that is, the HVO. We do not know the person to whom the document is addressed, whether it is the Defence Department, Mr. Ivica Lucic. We also don't know who it is that appears at the end of this letter in the signature block; is it Mr. Anto Sliskovic. The document bears several lines drawn by hand as well as certain notes in the margins. The document is dated the 15th of April, and as I was saying, on the list that we have it is indicated that the date of this document is the 25th of April. For these reasons, Mr. President, we believe that a witness is necessary for the Chamber to be able to derive the proper use from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is a document 419 on the Prosecutor list. I don't need the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My comments regarding this document are limited to saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you wish to respond? Document by document or globally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, there will obviously be a certain extent of repetition; however, the Prosecution would prefer to respond document by document, as we did last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. What do you have to say regarding document 157?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, very briefly. Document 157 stems from the Croatian State Archive. As all documents from the Croatian State Archive - and I have given explanations a few days ago - are photocopies only, and I have explained the procedure as to how such documents were received by the Office of the Prosecution. It's, however, an official document; it has the stamp of the Croatian State Archive on the top right-hand corner. The document is relevant. It concerns the kidnapping of Zivko Totic and the control of MOS members by the accused Hadzihasanovic. My learned friend from the Defence is right; there are handwritten remarks on the right-hand side of the document. And my learned friend also is right in saying that the document has a certain date which is not quite correctly reflected in our list. This is purely an oversight from our side. Again, that's probably an issue we will repeatedly discuss today. It only can touch on the probative value of the document but not on the admissibility of the document. And I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that Defence themselves recently have tendered into evidence, and it was admitted, a document in which significant portions were actually highlighted and an explanation couldn't be given. Therefore, again, it's the probative value only, but it can't touch the admissibility of the document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm returning the document. The second document, please, 419.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before addressing this document, 419, I just have one remark to make. With regard to each document, my learned friend goes back to saying that there's a question of the probative value and not its admissibility that is being addressed. And according to the representations made by the parties, we feel that all documents have to be a minimum of probative value to be admitted. And it is at this stage that the Defence is making these observations with regard to certain documents that don't have that minimum threshold of probative value without the support of additional evidence. Document 419. The observation of the Defence are limited to the fact that we only have a summary in the English language. We are of the opinion that all documents should be -- that are going to be tendered should be translated in full and that that complete translation should reflect each line of the document. That is our only remark regarding document 419. The next document, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. Mr. Withopf, document 419, the Defence is telling us that the English translation is provided only of the summary of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may please hand over the original of the document, which may be helpful in addressing this issue. Document 419 is the official response from the Cantonal Court in Zenica to an official OTP request for assistance in respect to the operation of the Zenica District Military Court. It's obviously highly relevant, since it contains information about the establishment of the Zenica District Military Court and the judges who worked there between January 1993 and March 1994. It makes reference and it provides information on war crime trials, and it also says in the document that in respect to BiH army members, not a single case was tried during the period in question. The issue as raised by my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence, this document has attached the exchange of letters between the Office of the Prosecutor and the Bosnian authorities, and it's my understanding that my learned friend from the Defence is referring to these letters in saying that no full translation was provided. The Prosecution, of course, if requested to do so, is certainly in a position to provide a translation of this letter exchange. Otherwise, I personally, with my limited knowledge of the B/C/S language, am not in a position to judge as to whether each line of the main document has been translated. If my learned friend, however, would tell us which line or lines are missing, we will take care of the full translation. It's my understanding, however, that the full translation of the document has been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have an interpreter at your disposal, so she can translate the text immediately for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have here the original that we are seeing for the first time, and we have just learned that this is a request from the OTP, which is something that we didn't know. The documents that we had consisted only of the letter and not the other documents. So we didn't even know that it was a request from the OTP. Looking at the serial number, we couldn't know that it came from the Prosecution. So we don't know whether there are other documents attached, because the original is quite different. There's a request from the OTP dated 2002, with the stamps and originals, and this letter as well. So, Mr. President, clearly, that this document is not complete. We only have the response, without knowing the context within which the document was produced. And that is why we need to have a witness present in the chamber to tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move on to the third document. Madam Usher, will you pick up the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 248, and we have the same observations to make with regard to that document. It's a document that is again a summary that has been translated. We are looking at the document, the translated document, which we received on two occasions: A summary and then a new copy with some additional comments regarding this document have to do with the passages that were highlighted. Perhaps we need to see the original document for this purpose. This is a document dated 1994, which appears to be similar in shape as the last document, because it was a request sent by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, will you pick up the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the document with me now, Mr. President. The document, Mr. President, comes from the military court in Travnik. The original doesn't give us more information regarding the context within which the document was produced. We know it is dated the 20th of May, 1993. As the Chamber is able to see, it is a document that the Defence may easily need. It could use this document, because this is a document relating to measures taken by the 3rd Corps. And true to our policy with regard to documents, we feel that such a document requires a witness for the Chamber to be able to use it. This document could have been used or at least shown to a witness that did appear in this courtroom. Those are the only observations that we have to make regarding document 248.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Document 248 is a document that stems from the Sarajevo collection and was received in a manner I have provided extensive information about. As my learned friend already mentioned, it's a letter of the Travnik District Military Court to 3rd Corps command making reference to information by Mehmed Alagic, the commander of the OG Bosanska Krajina about crimes committed by soldiers in Travnik and it details the activities of the court. It's my understanding, Mr. President, Your Honours, that a full, official CLSS translation has been provided, and I would please again ask my learned friend from the Defence to indicate which portions of the original document appear to be missing. And again, the Prosecution would be very happy to provide additional translations if necessary. In respect to the issue whether a witness is needed or not, the Prosecution maintains its view that even if the document is not discussed with a witness, it still has probative value and the probative value is certainly higher than the hurdle Defence is trying to use in respect to the non-admissibility of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fourth document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The next document is 91. It is a document dated the 1st of June. Could I see the original, please? The question that arises in this case, Mr. President, with respect to this document is that it is -- emanates from the Croatian Defence Council from the forward command post at Vitez. If we look on the list of addressees to whom this document was apparently sent, we see that it should have been sent to the commander of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army -- no, I'm sorry, to the 3rd Corps commander, to the commander of the HVO army, to the Monitoring Mission of the European Community, to the British Battalion situated at Bila, to the joint command of the army in Travnik, and also to the International Committee of the Red Cross. Mr. President, we have no information as to whether anyone received this document or not. On the original, there is one stamp, and from which we cannot see whether anyone received this document beyond the HVO. In order to derive any kind of use from this document, for it to have any probative value, we need to know whether the document was indeed sent and received by one of the entities to which it was addressed outside the HVO. The stamp could be a stamp of reception, which does not appear, which was not translated. Therefore, on the draft translation the stamp does not appear, whereas in the B/C/S version we do see the stamp. And from this, one might conclude that it was received on the 1st of June, but we don't know by whom. However, we do see letters "HS HVO" which probably means "the Supreme Command of the HVO." This was never seen by anyone outside, and if it was seen, Mr. President, we need to have a witness to tell us that for the Chamber to be able to use it. In the absence of that evidence, the document does not satisfy the minimum threshold to be admissible and to be of any use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall have a look at it. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, document 91 is an original copy of a document from the Croatian State Archive. It has the official stamp on the top right-hand corner. It contains information about wrongdoings of members of the ABiH in Travnik on 1st June 1993, obviously a few days prior to the main attack in the area on 8 June 1993. A witness is mentioned in this document who testified before this Tribunal in this trial and confirmed the allegations. In respect to the more technical issue, as mentioned by my learned friend, the stamp on the original actually has been translated. The contents of the stamp can be seen in the translation which is contained in the document binder. The document also says that it was submitted, number one, to the addressees. I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that this is a document that was received from the Croatian State Archive obviously indicating that the Croatian State Archive usually doesn't have the ABiH stamp on their documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, by your leave, I should simply like to underline that the stamp does not appear on the translation. What does appear on the translation is the last block of the letter just before the signature block with Tihomir Blaskic. That information does appear, but the stamp itself does not appear on the translation. Also, my learned friend has underlined something very important, and that is that one of the persons mentioned in this document did appear before this Chamber. My learned friend tells us that this witness confirmed what is contained in this document; then the document should have been tendered together with the witness. But to say today that the witness confirmed the content of the document is not sufficient for a document to be admitted when we don't know whether it was received by anyone at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fifth document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President. Mr. President, this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This witness is a protected witness, and we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, prepare an order to redact page 64, line 25, to redact the names, and line 22 as well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: If we look at the contents of this document, we don't see why the Prosecution is proposing a document dated 1997 about events that occurred in 1993; and, furthermore, a witness appeared in court and he was never questioned on this subject. The witness appeared under the pseudonym ZI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: First I wish to mention that this document was not on the most recent list of documents Defence indicated to discuss today. Otherwise, this is a document that stems from the Croatian State Archive in Zagreb, again an official document. It deals with the layout of the Muslim forces artillery. And although the document is dated the 28th of May, 1997, it's making reference, what's visible from page 2 of the document, to the situation on the 16th of April, 1993. Therefore, it's obviously a relevant document. The witness ZI -- as Your Honours certainly do recall, the examination of the witness ZI was limited to his Rule 82 bis statement, and the statement was limited to issues of destruction and looting in the area of Maljine, Guca Gora, Grahovcici, and all the other villages mentioned in the indictment. Therefore, there was no possibility for the Prosecution, no opportunity for the Prosecution to introduce this document and to present this document to Witness ZI. It still has sufficient probative value in the view of the Prosecution that it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon, would you like to conclude?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Those are the five documents I wanted to discuss before the Trial Chamber today. I only have two comments I would like to make about certain documents, first of all about the videos. We wouldn't like to draw your attention to each of the videos, but we have a list of all the videos that the Prosecution has tendered -- has included on its list, and we don't think that these videos should be admitted into evidence as the Prosecution suggests. When General Reinhardt was testifying here, we noted the lack of reliability of such documents. And, Mr. President, we don't think that the Trial Chamber should admit these documents into evidence in the situation they are in, in the state they are in. As far as the telephone conversations are concerned, as the Trial Chamber has noted, on two occasions in the course of a cross-examination we have used an intercept of a conversation between General Hadzihasanovic and General Halilovic, a conversation that took place in the headquarters of the army in Sarajevo. On two occasions we mentioned that this is a telephone intercept, and we're not sure whether this conversation really took place. There are a number of types of such conversations, of such intercepts. We don't know the purposes for which these intercepts were made. We know that these around aren't recordings, but a person took down notes, recorded it in written form. It's not an audio recording of the conversation. Could the Trial Chamber carefully examine the contents of these telephone conversations, because we believe given the state they have been recorded in, these conversations don't have sufficient probative value to be admitted. And finally, Mr. President, when we discussed the admissibility of documents, we cast doubt on the contents of the document and we said that certain documents shouldn't be admitted into evidence if this wasn't done through a witness, even if these documents could be used to the Defence's benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Unless -- is there something that Mr. Withopf would like to say about the videos and the telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President, Your Honours. The videos should not be dealt with in the generalised manner my learned friend from the Defence just did. The videos have probative value. The source for all the videos were disclosed -- the sources for all the videos were disclosed. Both the Trial Chamber and the Defence were informed about the source of such videos. The contents of the videos are self-explanatory to a very high extent, and I also wish to draw the attention to the Trial Chamber to the fact that Reinhardt -- General Reinhardt, the military expert, made only comments in respect to one particular video. The Prosecution is still of the view that the videos have probative value and therefore should be admitted, even without having a witness commenting on the contents of the videos. The intercepted phone conversations. Again, the Prosecution has provided detail as to how these phone conversations, copies of the intercepted phone conversations were received. My learned friend from the Defence has pointed out that Defence themselves have repeatedly used these telephone conversations; and even today, the today's witness was made to make comments on particular portions of such telephone conversations. Therefore, the position of the Defence is a bit contradictory. Otherwise, the Prosecution, we think that although these copies -- or although the contents of these document are handwritten, obviously they still have sufficient probative value in order to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dixon, I will give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to address the categories that I've handed to Your Honours and to my learned friends from the Prosecution. Before I do that, Your Honours, there's one general point which we wish to make, and that is in response to the submission that was made by my learned friend from the Prosecution that these are official documents and that they therefore have a reliability which allows them to be admitted. He mentioned that as one of the factors for yourself to take into account. Your Honour, we would accept that within national jurisdictions documents that come from official bodies and governmental authorities usually do carry with them a presumption of their reliability, and in most domestic courts they will not, therefore, need to be authenticated. However, we are here in an international court where documents from various domestic jurisdictions often end up before Your Honours, and in our view the way in which those documents are to be admitted cannot be equated with how it occurs in a domestic system. Your Honours, in our submission, we cannot accept documents purely on the basis that they appear on their face to be official documents, and it's for that reason that we have requested - and I think my learned friend has conceded this - that we require at least somebody from the government archive or from the different archives that are involved to come before Your Honours to testify as to the manner in which these various official documents were collected, and indeed, then became official documents. We have already indicated that in respect of the 7th Brigade archive there are questions which we wish to raise about how that archive came to exist; who had access to that archive; and whether documents that ended up in that archive were indeed documents of the 7th Brigade, whether they were ever sent from the 7th Brigade or received by the 7th Brigade. The same applies to the Sarajevo archive as well. And we believe such a witness or witnesses would assist Your Honours in deciding on the official status of these documents. In our view, it is not sufficient simply to assert that they are official in order to have them admitted as exhibits. Your Honour, turning to the categories. If I may begin by looking at all the documents that concern signatures, those being ones in Category B, C, and H. There are four documents altogether, and I would ask that the originals of all of them be made available at once. That's document number 8, 37, 56, and 103. They can be looked at together because they all concern the same topic of signatures, and it might save us some time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm going to hand over these four documents in a few seconds. If I please may be permitted to make a few remarks to what has just been said by my learned friend from the Kubura Defence. The Prosecution has a number of times informed the Trial Chamber and the Defence that we have the intention and will interview the archivist or archivists of a number of archives. And this is certainly an issue I would like to address later on today once we've finished the discussion on the specific documents, since the Prosecution is seeking some guidance from the Trial Chamber in that respect. Otherwise, the issue of official documents has been repeatedly addressed. Defence themselves have repeatedly in tendering documents into evidence referred to the fact that these are official documents and such documents were received by the Defence from the very same archives as they were received by the Prosecution, and the Trial Chamber has repeatedly accepted the fact that a document on its face appears to be an official document makes it admissible. In respect to the 7th Muslim Brigade archive - that's the now-7th Mechanised Brigade archive in Zenica - I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that only very few of such documents are included in the Prosecution's exhibit list. I'm now going to provide the originals of the four documents that were just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution wants documents 8, 56, 157 -- 57 [as interpreted] and 103 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 37, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you fetch the original, please. Document 8 is dated the 12th of April, 1993. It is from the 7th Brigade, and it is addressed to Mr. Kordic. Document number 37 is dated the 23rd of July, 1993. It's an order assigning four individuals. Document number 56 is the code of conduct for the 7th Brigade. It is dated the 1st of November, 1994. And document number 103 is a list of soldiers who were members of the 7th Brigade. It's a list of soldiers but of officers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: If I may begin with contested Exhibit Number 8, Your Honour. As Your Honour has indicated, this is a letter purportedly sent by the commander of the 7th Brigade to Mr. Kordic on the 2nd of April, 1993. Our dispute with this document is in relation to the signature, Your Honour. This is not the signature of Mr. Kubura. In future documents that I show Your Honours, his signature will become evident, and it's quite clearly a different signature to the one on this document. In addition to that, we have no name of the person who signed it. We simply have what seems to be a signature and then the word "commander of the 7th Brigade." In the other documents in this category, Category B, there is at least a name mentioned when one sees the signature and "commander of 7th Brigade." However, in this document there isn't even an author of the document identified. Your Honour, in our submission, this document should not be admitted unless a witness can attend to verify who signed this document and to permit us to ask that person questions about whether or not they were authorised to sign such a document, if indeed this document was an official one of the 7th Brigade. In our view, Your Honour, the probative value of this document is minimal unless such a witness is called. In our submission, Your Honours would not be able to rely on this document in any meaningful way unless it could be confirmed as a document which did indeed come from the 7th Brigade. We have gone through these submissions before, but to summarise again, Your Honours, this is essentially a piece of hearsay evidence. Your Honours will being asked to look at a document where the author of the document is not before Your Honours to give their evidence firsthand. So it is a piece of documentary hearsay. Of course hearsay evidence is admissible before the ICTY, but as Your Honours have indicated on numerous occasions, the source of that hearsay should be known to Your Honours and to the parties if it is to be admitted. That is important, Your Honours, in order to establish the reliability of the hearsay evidence and in order to be able to determine what weight to give it thereafter in Your Honours' assessments. In our view, unless the source of the document is at least identified and known to Your Honours, such hearsay evidence - albeit in a documentary form - should not be admitted. Here the source of the document isn't known; the author isn't known. And in our submission, it should therefore be excluded, unless that source does become known through a witness to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you fetch the document. I'd like to look at something. I'd like to check something. And then I will let Mr. Withopf take the floor. Mr. Dixon didn't mention the fact that at the bottom and to the left there is a stamp. It's in B/C/S. It mentions "sent." They have the date, the 2nd of April, 1993, at 16.10 hours, 1610 hours. Then it mentions how it was sent, either by telex or by telegram, by telephone, by radio communications, or by wire. And something has been encircled. And this probably indicates how the document was sent or forwarded. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, you already addressed a number of facts I would like to address a bit more. But first to the authenticity of this document. This is an official document of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade seized as a result of the consensual search in the ABiH main archive in Sarajevo. The document is obviously signed. The document is highly relevant. It's a letter of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade commander of the 2nd of April, 1993 at a point in time the accused Kubura was already acting commander to the HVO commander Dario Kordic. And the letter speaks about "foreign nationals, volunteers in our ranks." This was a quote. The issue about the signature. It has a signature. The document, it may or may not be the accused Kubura's signature. It on its face is a very official document, as Your Honour Mr. Presiding Judge already pointed out; it has two official stamps on it, namely the stamp of the 7th Muslim Brigade and another official stamp of the 3rd Corps. The author of the document is known; it's the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. The source is known; it's the commander, and we informed the Trial Chamber where the document was found. And the fact that the Prosecution wishes to use or wishes to prove with this document does not depend on the fact or on the issue as to whether a name is attached to the word "Commander 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade." Therefore, the Prosecution is of the view this document is of probative value and should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go on to document number 37. And could both parties please proceed expeditiously, because I see that time is passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will move on to document 37 now. My only response in respect of contested document number 8 is that we're not disputing that this document was sent somewhere. That's evident on the bottom of the document. It's just who sent the document and whether that was indeed somebody within the 7th Brigade, so that this document can in any way be relied upon by Your Honours. In our submission, this is not the signature of Mr. Kubura and therefore should not be admitted into evidence which can potentially be evidence that is used against him at some point. Your Honours, contested document 37 and 56, these are two documents which refer to signatures other than those of Mr. Kubura. The first one being contested exhibit 37, is a document purportedly signed by Mr. Koricic in his capacity, here, it says, as the brigade commander, and that is of the 7th Brigade on the 23rd of July, 1993. In our submission - and the point is the same as the one that I made earlier - this document can be of no use to Your Honours unless the person who authored the document or somebody can authenticate that this document was indeed one which proposed the appointment of these persons. We would also ask Your Honours to take note that the Prosecution has never alleged that Mr. Koricic was the brigade commander, and yet here they're seeking to rely upon a document purportedly signed by him in that capacity. And in our submission that, blatant contradiction must mean that the document is unreliable and should not be admitted into evidence, unless the witness is called. Your Honours, I can deal with contested exhibit 56 at the same time, and then my friend can respond to both. That will save time. 56 is the code of conduct of the 7th Brigade signed by a soldier. Once again, the person is identified but this person is not being called as a witness to verify that this is indeed the code of conduct of the 7th Brigade. And most importantly, it's a document signed on the 1st of November, 1994, which is long after the time when Mr. Kubura was the commander of the 7th Brigade. So once again, of what possible assistance could it be to Your Honours in trying to resolve questions relating to the time period when Mr. Kubura was the commander? This may not be the code of conduct of the 7th Brigade at all at the relevant time. In addition, there's one further point in relation to this document. Having seen the original now, Your Honours, I note that on the back of the document there is a typed and written script which was not included in the documents that we received and not translated. So I have no idea what is on the back of this document. It's the first time I've seen this now. That matter could of course be resolved through the Prosecution translating the document for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, could you briefly comment on documents number 37 and 56. Could you do so in a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, both documents were received as a result of the consensual search, obviously. 37 is relevant. It's the proposal for the appointment of the accused Kubura as the brigade commander, and it also includes Serif Patkovic, known from the testimony from a number of witnesses in these proceedings. And it's making reference to his appointment of Chief of Staff; obviously relevant. The technical issue: It appears to be very normal that a different person than the one who was proposed to be appointed as commander signs such a document. The main issue, however, is it's again an official document of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade; therefore, the Prosecution is of the view that this document has probative value, even without the author of the document testifying about the document. Moving on to document 56. It's relevant. Also, it's a 1994 document. It makes reference to the "Instructions to the Muslim Fighter," a booklet which is marked for identification as a Prosecution exhibit, published in 1993, obviously during the time period of the indictment. And reference is made extensively in paragraph 70 of the indictment. And the code of conduct which is addressed in document 56 is explicitly making reference to the instructions to the Muslim fighter. Of course, it's a receipt that a soldier signed, an ABiH 3rd Corps 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade soldier in 1994. That's certainly correct. However, as we have mentioned repeatedly, this is a case in which bits and pieces of evidence will be put together and this is just another piece of evidence. And the Prosecution is of the view that in combination with other documents, it has probative value and should be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on now, please, to 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, to take this swiftly, our basic point is that this document does not have any stamp. It is not signed. It is an example of a documents that unsigned. It is simply a collection of four pages of names without a date, and in our submission we cannot possibly see the reliability and relevance of this document to Your Honours in deciding any of the issues in the case. And for that reason, it should not be admitted, unless a witness can come and explain what this document is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very briefly: It's correct, the document doesn't have a signature. However, it's an official document; again, stemming from Sarajevo collection 1, and it has been searched and seized from the archives of the 7th Mechanised Brigade in Zenica, obviously the successor brigade of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. As mentioned, it's correct there is no signature. As one can see from the original, this is obviously a computer print. It's not an order. It's not a report. It's a document which by its nature is typically not signed. Therefore, the Prosecution is still of the view that this document has probative value and should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue for the other categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The documents concerning signature s can now be handed to Your Honours, if you wish to view them, and returned. There's only one other document, Your Honour, that I would need to look at the original. The others I can do now without referring to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us the numbers of those documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: That's document 65 is the only other document that I will ask Your Honours' permission to look at the original of. I'll refer to some other documents, but I will do that without needing to have the original before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 65 is dated the 8th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a report about the unacceptable conduct of some members of the 7th Brigade, signed by Mr. Koricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If the original could be obtained, and then I will address Your Honours briefly on this document which we've put in the category of "confusing documents." And I think Your Honour will hopefully appreciate why we have indicated that it is a document that we cannot make any sense of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English translation, it says "for the commander," and in the B/C/S document there's a small word just in front of the word "komandant."

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The original is here. I will pass that up to Your Honours. Your Honours, our essential submission on this document is that if the English translation is looked at, as Your Honours indicated, this is a report about alleged unacceptable conduct of the 7th Brigade. It's not coming from the 7th Brigade but a report from the commander of a particular military unit, which is indicated at the top of the document. When Your Honours turn over to the second page, however, we see a separate document which is signed by Mr. Koricic, an order of 6 April 1993. In our submission, there's no clear connection between these two pages. They appear to be two unrelated pages, as opposed to one document. The second page has got a number of 04414-1 at the top. That's the document of 6 April 1993. And it's a number referring to a previous report; on the basis of a previous report this order is then issued by Mr. Koricic. However, Your Honours, when the first page of the document is looked at - the number on that is "48293," and it's 8 April 1993, so a date after this order is allegedly sent out by Mr. Koricic - so on its face there appears to be in connection between the two pages, and indeed the first page is unsigned. There's no signature on it. And in our view, given that it is impossible to make sense of how these two documents fit together, failing a witness explaining it, they should not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The problem is a very simple one. There are two documents which are copies of an original document which was typed. When the documents were seized, people didn't realise that these related to two different events. There's an order dated the 6th of April, and then there's a report dated the 8th of April. And when the two documents were seized, they must have been one next to another and perhaps the investigator didn't pay attention to these matters. What are you telling us, Mr. Withopf?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's certainly correct, both the observations of you, The Presiding Judge, and my learned friend from the Kubura Defence. These two documents on their face appear to be confusing. The original may indicate that it is one and the same document; however, nobody obviously can be sure about. And as my learned friend from the Defence pointed out, reference is made to a report, 6th of April, and the report is dated 8th of April, 1993. However, what appears to be important in discussing the admissibility of this document is the fact that both the report and the order deal with the very same issue, namely the radical behaviour of some members of the 7th Muslim Brigade in the 8 April report, and the order which prohibits any kind of extremist behaviour. So the documents are certainly linked to each other, and the Prosecution suggests that both documents separately and together have probative value and therefore should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's continue. Let's move on. I shall return the document to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kubura's signature is on that document. Your Honours may wish to consult that in order to compare it to the documents in Category B, which are not signed by Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Koricic, isn't it, not Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, for and on behalf of Mr. Kubura, Koricic is signing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that it was Mr. Kubura who signed on behalf of Mr. Koricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Indeed, your, and that is Mr. Kubura's signature there. There's no dispute with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are recognising the reality of the second document. Mr. Withopf, the Defence tells us that on the second document we have the signature of Mr. Kubura in the original, which is no longer contested, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no dispute that our contestation of these documents or document was with the fact that the two were put together and there's no connection on their face. And hence, it was a confusing document, which we said should not be admitted in the form that the Prosecution had put forward. Simple as that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no observation to make on this statement, which appears to be quite an interesting one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no further originals to show Your Honours. But going through the rest of the categories, starting with Category A, which are documents outside the time frame of the charges, there are two documents we wish to refer Your Honours to, and those are contested exhibit 4 and contested exhibit 6. Both of these relate, as Your Honours will see, to the music school. The first is a document dated 15 January 1993 regarding the establishment of a detention centre for Bosnian soldiers at the music school, and the second concerns investigations into crimes against certain Bosnian soldiers who are held at the music school. In our view, there is no possible relevance of these documents to the crimes that the Prosecution alleges occurred after 1 April 1993 at the music school, and these documents should not be admitted in a period before Mr. Kubura became the commander unless the Prosecution can show what is the connection between these documents and crimes that were allegedly committed by subordinates of Mr. Kubura while he was the commander. Your Honour, I've gone through this argument before, and I don't wish to tramp over ground that we've covered already. They are simply examples of how there are a number of documents listed in Category A which we say have no bearing on their face to the charges, and they should not be admitted unless the Prosecution can discharge its burden of showing why these documents are linked to their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is simple: This is a problem of relevance with respect to the time frame of the indictment. The Defence tells us that these documents have dates which do not fit within the time frame of the indictment. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I don't know whether Your Honours wish to have the original of the document in front of them prior to discussing the document. Due to the nature of the challenge, I wouldn't deem it to be necessary, but I'm happy to provide you with the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Both documents, in the view of the Prosecution, are relevant. The one document dated the 15th of January, 1993, in paragraph 8, it says: "In the music school --" and it's making reference to the Zenica Music School -- "established a military detention unit." It's the view of the Prosecution that the fact that the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade themselves order the establishment of a detention unit in the Zenica Music School is highly relevant. It proves that following the 15th of January, 1993 there was an ABiH 3rd Corps 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade detention facility in the Zenica Music School, at least together with additional evidence which shows that at a later point in time when the accused Kubura was in charge of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. In combination with such additional evidence it certainly has probative value and should be admitted. Document 6, very briefly. The document shows that the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had the capability to investigate crimes if they were willing to do so. The fact that they were able to do so on 3 March 1993 already and only about four weeks prior to the accused Kubura being appointed as acting commander is obviously significant, and it appears in addition to being significant that the document was copied to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade Chief of Staff, who at the time was the accused Kubura. In the original, this line is actually underlined. Therefore, the Prosecution is of the view that this document has probative value, if not even high probative value, and therefore it should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. One point in response. None of the points that my learned friend has made are disputed by the Defence team for Mr. Kubura. And as I indicated earlier on to Your Honours, evidence should only be admitted if it goes to points in dispute in the case. There's no need to admit evidence that goes to matters where there's no issue that Your Honours have to decide as the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, the next category is "handwritten documents." The numbers referred to there are all ones that relate to the war diary, the 3rd Corps war diary. And there are a few other documents as well. There's no need for me, Your Honours, to show Your Honours any copies of that diary, save to say that it is a form of hearsay evidence to admit the diary without knowing the source of the person who wrote the diary and giving the Defence an opportunity to cross-examine that person as to whether or not they recorded events properly and correctly as they occurred in the meetings. So we would request a witness for the 3rd Corps diary. Your Honour, in Category C, before I move on to the final few categories, I do wish to mention that although Your Honours might think there are a lot of numbers there, a lot of witnesses would need to be called, indeed the numbers overlap to some extent with the same author of the documents appearing on a number of occasions. So there is, for example, one person who authored ten of these documents; another who authored seven; another who authored nine. And although many numbers appear there, it might mean that only four or five witnesses are required to cover all of those documents. Category E, Your Honour, which is El-Liva magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Regarding Category C first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may just briefly respond. I understand that we are going document by document. The war diaries -- the two war diaries have repeatedly been address. I really do not want to repeat everything that has been said. Both were seized as a result of the October 2000 searches. They stem from the ABiH main archive in Sarajevo, Sarajevo collection 1. Document 28 - that's the document actually my learned friend is referring to - these are respective portions of the 23rd of June, 1993. These appear to be minutes of a meeting held on exactly that day with both the accused Hadzihasanovic and the accused Kubura being present. The accused Kubura is quoted with a proposal "hiring foreign nationals, and we will continue to hire them because they receive ammunition." Obviously, quite highly relevant. The technical issue which has been in particularly addressed by my learned friend, handwritten document. I already made my comments in that respect repeatedly. It's the very nature of such a war diary that it is in handwriting, and in this case the Prosecution is of the view that there's no witness needed because of that fact. Certainly the document has probative value by the very nature of this document and it should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next category, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The magazine. In our submission, we do not challenge the existence of this magazine. It's simply the contents of what is written in the magazine and require a witness to be cross-examined about what they have stated in order to test the reliability of that information and its credibility. And it's for that reason that we would require a witness for any evidence that is to be used from that magazine. Otherwise, we are really accepting the stories of journalists, which in our submission could be of very little assistance to Your Honours in deciding the real issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the magazines, those that appear to come directly from the 3rd Corps or the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, as mentioned earlier on, the El-Liva magazine is an open-source document and it is the official magazine of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And if I may please draw the attention of Your Honours and the Defence to page 2 of the El-Liva magazine, which is document 54, it says, obviously in the B/C/S language "Izdavac 7 Muslimanska Brigada," and I did a quick inquiry what this actually means, and it says "Publisher, 7th Muslim Brigade." The Prosecution is certainly very willing to provide an official translation of this particular portion of the El-Liva magazine, which appears to appear in all of the El-Liva magazines the Prosecution is suggesting to tender into evidence. El-Liva was the official magazine of the 7th Muslim Brigade. To our knowledge, the first edition was published in February 1993 and it was still published at the end of 1995 and possibly later. Again, since the El-Liva magazine is an official 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade magazine, it is of high probative value and certainly of such a probative value that it should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any more categories, Mr. Dixon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other category that I do wish to refer to is G, "Videos." I have already referred Your Honours to number 409, being a video supposedly of the formation of the 7th Brigade in August of 1992, when the Prosecution in its own indictment alleges that that took place in November 1992. And video 87 was the video, portions of which were shown to General Reinhardt. In our submission, the cross-examination of him, albeit only on a part, did show that what is seen on those videos, the images that are captured are not necessarily verified, either in the transcript or in any other source provided by the Prosecution. They've indicated where they got the video but not what we see in the video. And I agree with my learned friend that you cannot lump all of the videos together, but in our submission it would be necessary to go through them all to determine whether anything that is shown on them can be of any value to Your Honours before they are admitted into evidence. Those are the only two examples that I do wish to refer to. After my learned friend has replied, there are one or two general comments that I wish to make, and then I'll be completed in five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The videos, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can keep my answer very short, since I already made the Prosecution's observations on the videos, and I do not wish to again repeat them. I'm making reference to what I said earlier on today. I wish, however, to point out that transcripts of the audio of the video have been provided to both the Trial Chamber and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm told that we have to have the break in five minutes. I would have preferred as to finish in continuity, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will complete my submissions. There are no further categories that I wish to refer Your Honours to. The document numbers are there, so Your Honours are able to see which are the different documents that we do contest. In our submission, Your Honours, much of what has happened throughout this debate centres on whether or not a degree of probative value should be shown before a document is admitted, value both in the sense of its reliability and its relevance. There are two possible options or views that can be taken: Either that the threshold is very low or non-existent. And in fact, Your Honours as professional Judges can determine the relevance of evidence in light of all the evidence and weigh its weight accordingly. But another view, and the one which we have sought to put forward to Your Honours, is that before evidence is admitted, a threshold must be met so that only evidence that can be shown to be linked to a relevant issue in the case, an issue in dispute, should be admitted. And there should also be a threshold of reliability. That does not mean, Your Honours, that documents that are not admitted at this stage can't be admitted at a later stage. As I've indicated before, these documents are always marked for identification, and it's entirely possible that they can be admitted at a later point when their reliability or relevance does become known, either through a witness or because of other evidence presented. We have asked for a number of witnesses to attend in these categories, and that remains our submission. I would, however, add that if Your Honours are against us on these points, that you do take our submissions into account when considering the weight to be given to these documents at a later point. The challenges we make as to admissibility equally apply to the weight to be given to these documents. Thank you, Your Honours, for the opportunity to go through these categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Finally, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has made all its comments and all its observations on the more general issues, and the Prosecution has repeatedly expressed its view that the approach as was taken by the Kvocka Trial Chamber should be applied in this case as well. I'm making reference to all the submissions I made in respect to the more general questions as addressed by my learned friend from the Kubura Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you would like to say something? But very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. First of all, the Chamber during the debate on the documents has noted that there's a system of numbering, especially the orders in the headquarters. We still have no information regarding this system of numbering, though we could have at least heard the opinion of an expert to tell us how this could function in a military headquarters. The question of authorisation of documents, production of documents, signature, and dispatch, probably this functions similarly in all military headquarters, but we have no information on that subject. Another very important remark, Mr. President, has to do with the quantity of documents that have been produced and for which the Prosecution is asking that they be admitted today. I haven't verified in all the other cases, but it has never been seen to such an extent that the Prosecution is asking for such a large number of documents to be admitted. I have come across some 40 or 50 documents. The Defence would like to thank the Chamber for allowing it to present its arguments regarding these documents, but it has to note that the Prosecution, which wishes to make up for shortcomings in its case, is endeavouring to throw 600 documents into the file to make up for this. One wonders how the Chamber will be able to use all those documents without having the benefit of the support of a testimony. Finally, Mr. President, we feel that the test that should be used to determine the minimum threshold of probative value is to see whether the Chamber can make any conclusion on the basis of a document without having to speculate on any part of that document. Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you for allowing us to present our arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf wishes to intervene in response of what has just been said. Perhaps to tell us about next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I will certainly at a later point in time give you information in respect to the witnesses of next week. However, if I may respectfully ask the Trial Chamber to have a short break, since the Prosecution wants to address after a short break the issue I mentioned earlier on. We are inclined to interview the archivists of the various archives; however, we wish to have some sort of guidance from the Trial Chamber, and in particular against the background that the Prosecution intends to close its case not later than during second week of June at the latest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber had planned to render its decision as soon as possible, as early as Monday, and then the question of archivists would be resolved as of Monday. So it's not very useful at this stage for us to address this question of archivists, because as you know, the Chamber has been thinking things over and discussing the matter amongst ourselves. If we have a break, the technical break lasts half an hour, and we have to close in three-quarters of an hour. So let us hear what you have to say about next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, in acknowledging what you just said, the Prosecution certainly doesn't need a break, and we may revisit this issue at a later point in time. Mr. President, Your Honours, in respect to the witnesses, can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of May, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.06 p.m.,
